Background

Conflicts of interest (CoI) can undermine trust in scientific publishing, yet empirical evidence on how often CoI lead to editorial action and how journals respond remains limited. This study aimed to characterise the frequency, patterns, and editorial handling of CoI‑related notices in the scholarly literature using an openly available, multidisciplinary dataset.

Methods

We conducted a descriptive cross‑sectional analysis of publicly available records from the Retraction Watch (RW) database, accessed via Crossref, from inception to 23 April 2026. All editorial notices in which CoI was explicitly mentioned as the sole or one of several stated reasons were included, encompassing retractions, corrections, expressions of concern, and reinstatements. For each record, we extracted article and notice dates, article type, scientific field, country of the corresponding author, number of authors and institutions, publisher, and all stated reasons for the notice. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and bootstrap‑based confidence intervals.

Results

We identified 886 CoI‑related records (748 retractions, 39 corrections, 97 expressions of concern, and 2 reinstatements). CoI was the sole stated reason in 95 cases (10.7%), including 32 retractions, 11 corrections, and 52 expressions of concern; in the remaining notices, CoI most commonly co‑occurred with concerns such as compromised peer review, authorship or affiliation problems, journal or institutional investigations, and broader ethical violations. The median time from publication to editorial action was longest for expressions of concern and shortest for corrections, with wide variability across records and notice types. CoI‑related notices were concentrated in basic life, biomedical, and health sciences, and were unevenly distributed across high‑output countries and a small number of large publishers, particularly open‑access outlets. Most affected articles were original research papers with multi‑author, multi‑institution teams. Among articles with determinable author gender, both first and last authors were more often male than female, although these patterns were exploratory and lacked a baseline comparator.

Conclusions

Editorial actions explicitly linked to CoI remain relatively uncommon compared with the broader volume of retractions and corrections, and CoI are rarely cited in isolation. The frequent co‑occurrence of CoI with other forms of misconduct or procedural problems suggests that undisclosed or poorly managed CoI often signal deeper weaknesses in disclosure practices, editorial oversight, and research governance rather than isolated administrative lapses. Strengthening CoI policies, transparency, verification mechanisms, and linked metadata systems may help detect problems earlier and support more consistent, graduated editorial responses.","affiliation":"Department of Pathology, Forensic Medicine & Cytology, University Hospital of Split, Split, Croatia. Introduction

Lateral crural strut grafts are versatile cartilage grafts that provide improved lateral wall support and can be used to correct post-rhinoplasty deformities such as alar retraction.

Objective and hypothesis

The objective of this paper is to review the indications and techniques used for lateral crural strut grafts and lateral crural extension grafts for treating alar retraction.

Study design

Description of surgeon's technique and case examples for use of lateral crural strut grafts and lateral crural extension grafts for managing alar retraction.

Methods

Techniques demonstrated through intraoperative photography, case examples, and videos.

Results

Patient outcomes as evaluated in previously published clinical experience with lateral crural strut grafts and lateral crural extension grafts.

Conclusion

Lateral crural strut grafts and lateral crural extension grafts provide excellent lateral wall support and are critical to the correction of alar retraction in secondary Scientific misconduct exploits the very mechanisms through which science establishes credibility, yet scientific correction is still commonly reduced to retraction counts. Retractions, however, represent only one observable manifestation of a far more complex regulatory system. Here, we develop a multidimensional systems-level framework for understanding scientific correction across the global scientific enterprise immediately before the emergence of AI-driven scientific governance. Integrating publication and retraction data from the 58 largest national scientific systems during 1900–2025, we examine three interconnected dimensions of correction architecture: the dynamics of scientific correction itself, its macro-structural organization, and its political-economic configuration. To support this framework, we introduce new multidimensional indicators, including the Normalized Retraction Rate and Duration Index (NRRDI) and the Normalized Retraction Rate and Slope13 Index (NRS13I). Our analyses suggest that scientific correction is intrinsically multidimensional, comprising distinct but interconnected dimensions of retraction burden, correction latency, collaboration-dependent correction structure, and early correction concentration dynamics. Across national systems, higher observable correction frequency was consistently associated with shorter correction latency, suggesting that correction visibility and correction responsiveness represent complementary manifestations of regulatory capacity rather than simple indicators of scientific dysfunction. The findings further reveal a pronounced East–West bipolarity in the global geography of scientific correction: retraction burden was concentrated disproportionately within Eastern and Middle Eastern scientific systems, whereas prolonged correction latency was concentrated predominantly within Western systems. This dissociation motivated the Retraction Cascade Hypothesis (RCH), which proposes that historically elevated correction visibility may amplify future correction concentration through self-reinforcing surveillance and anomaly-detection processes. Strikingly, academic freedom exhibited one of the strongest and most consistent inverse associations with retraction burden and displayed a closely parallel geographic pattern, suggesting that global correction asymmetries arise not only from surveillance amplification but also from deeper differences in epistemic-governance environments. More broadly, scientific correction emerged as a structurally embedded property of national scientific systems linked to governance quality, human development, institutional coherence, and epistemic openness. Governance-related and human-capital dimensions consistently exhibited stronger associations with correction-system organization than economic scale alone, although substantial residual heterogeneity indicated that important components of correction dynamics remain only partially predictable from macro-structural conditions. Across all three analytical dimensions, countries organized into distinct latent global correction regimes characterized by different combinations of developmental conditions, governance architecture, collaboration structure, and corrective visibility. Political-economic analyses demonstrated that scientific correction exposure scales super-proportionally with economic and research-investment scale, while increased R&D intensity did not significantly attenuate this relationship. At the same time, several comparatively low-cost scientific systems exhibited high efficiency-adjusted publication productivity despite elevated correction exposure, indicating that economic efficiency and integrity stability are not synonymous organizational properties. Importantly, although the political economy of scientific correction provides valuable insight into correction-system organization, reducing scientific correction primarily to economic loss would constitute a substantial conceptual oversimplification. The measurable financial exposure associated with retractions remains proportionally negligible relative to broader research investment and likely represents only the visible component of a much larger epistemic problem whose hidden scientific, societal, and potentially economic consequences remain difficult to quantify. Together, these findings support a reconceptualization of scientific correction as an adaptive layer of epistemic governance rather than a simple accumulation of isolated retractions. Correction mechanisms appear not merely as retrospective instruments of error removal, but as structurally organized processes through which scientific systems regulate credibility, transparency, accountability, and epistemic self-correction under varying institutional and developmental conditions. By establishing a multidimensional empirical baseline for the pre-AI era, this study provides a foundation for evaluating how artificial intelligence may reshape the architecture of scientific self-regulation in the decades ahead.

Purpose

To assess use of the novel spacer filamentous knitted polyester fabric (FKPF) in lid retraction correction in thyroid eye disease (TED) as an effective surgical method to preserve eyelid function and cosmesis.

Methods

A prospective, non-comparative interventional study of surgical outcomes in 30 patients with TED cases over a period of 3 years. The upper and lower eyelid retraction was corrected surgically with FKPF material. All intervention performed in the inactive phase of Rundle's curve plotting. LPS was partially recessed and resected from the central part of the tarsal plate to implant the FKPF material. Pre- and post-operative evaluation parameters were marginal reflex distance-1 (MRD-1), MRD-2, upper and lower scleral show, palpebral fissure height (PFH), and LPS action. All the patients were post-operatively followed up on the 1 st week, 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year.

Results

Pre-operative measurements to post-operative results revealed: MRD-1 was reduced from 9.73 ± 0.71 mm to 3.85 ± 0.51 mm; scleral show of upper lid reduced from 3.70 ± 0.71 mm to no scleral show; MRD-2 was reduced from 6.40 ± 1.18 mm to 5.38 ± 0.41 mm; scleral show of lower lid improved from 1.93 ± 0.36 mm to no scleral show. PFH was reduced from 16.07 ± 1.42 mm to 9.23 ± 0.73 mm. LPS action was pre-operatively 19.08 ± 1.20 mm to 14.40 ± 0.73 mm post-operatively.

Conclusion

FKPF is an inert, readily available, cost-effective material that shows promise in lid retraction correction. In our study, all lid retractions were repaired with no post-operative complications and met the functional and cosmetic purposes of the intervention. All patients reported high satisfaction with the outcome of the procedure.
